title: Rewire and reset are all you need: Minimal resources for manipulating non-Abelions
authors: Chiu Fan Bowen Lo, Rohith Sajith, Anasuya Lyons, Ashvin Vishwanath, Ruben Verresen
abstract: Braiding and fusing anyons are fundamental to topological quantum computation, yet existing circuit protocols often employ ancillas and measurements. We determine the minimal circuit resources for performing such anyon operations in quantum double models of generic finite groups. Our approach braids anyons through a sequential unitary circuit without ancillas. Intuitively, this is obtained by deforming the underlying graph on which the anyons live. More generally, we introduce graph rewiring, a diagrammatic calculus that assigns a geometric interpretation to individual two-qudit gates and tracks their action on stabilizers. For fusion, we prove a general no-go theorem excluding purely unitary protocols for fusing unknown anyon types without introducing ancillas. Remarkably, we show such "input-agnostic" fusion is enabled by simply using a qudit reset. Hence, contrary to folklore, ancilla resources are not needed to braid or fuse non-Abelian anyons (non-Abelions). This work has implications in experimental efforts in error correction: our fusion protocol highlights reset as an underutilized primitive for error correction without the spacetime-overhead of ancillas and measurements.
summary: This paper establishes that manipulating non-Abelian anyons, crucial for topological quantum computation, requires surprisingly few resources. By introducing 'graph rewiring,' the authors prove that both braiding and fusion can be achieved using only unitary gates and a simple qudit reset. This result significantly lowers the resource overhead estimates for fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_problem: Determining the minimal circuit resources required for performing fundamental non-Abelian anyon operations, specifically braiding and fusion, in topological quantum computation.
main_result: Ancilla qubits and measurements are not necessary for braiding or performing input-agnostic fusion of non-Abelian anyons, provided the operations are supplemented by a simple qudit reset.
method: The authors introduce 'graph rewiring,' a novel diagrammatic calculus, to geometrically interpret and track the action of two-qudit gates on the stabilizers of the underlying topological model.
model_or_system: The work analyzes non-Abelian anyons arising from the quantum double models D(G) of finite groups G, which are implemented on a lattice structure defined by stabilizer operators.
key_observables: Braiding paths, fusion outcomes, circuit resource requirements (unitary gates, reset, ancillas, measurements), and coherence preservation.
important_parameters: The structure of the finite group G, the type of anyon (irreducible representation of D(G)), and the presence/absence of reset operations.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the ability to model the system using quantum double models and assumes that the reset operation acts as a sufficient primitive to bypass the limitations of purely unitary fusion protocols.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the circuit resource classes, showing sequential circuits suffice for braiding, and that adding a reset enables input-agnostic fusion. Other figures detail the elementary rewiring moves and the steps for coherent flux movement using ancillas.
paper_structure: The paper develops the graph rewiring calculus, proves a no-go theorem for unitary fusion, and then demonstrates that combining rewiring with a reset operation achieves both braiding and fusion protocols with minimal resources.
why_interesting: The finding that reset can replace ancillas for fusion is highly relevant for experimental quantum computing platforms (like superconducting circuits) where minimizing overhead and resource consumption is critical for scaling error correction.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Circuit resource classes and the tasks they enable. A sequential circuit (blue) suffices to braid anyons a and b at different sites. Adding a reset primitive (red) allows input- agnostic fusion of a and b into c, leaving no anyon behind at the original site of a. This cannot be done with only uni- tary circuit without assuming knowledge on the input state. Adding measurement or an ancilla (green) allows syndrome extraction: the anyon type c at a site is measured and read out as a classical outcome.
